title: Secure Kotlin Programming
learning_outcomes: Explain the central rule or purpose of secure kotlin programming using at least one correct term from the lesson.
Interpret or adapt a small Kotlin example that demonstrates secure kotlin programming.
Identify one relevant edge case, debugging step, or version/platform constraint.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn **Secure Kotlin Programming** as part of **Software Engineering, Security, and Performance**. Treat external input, dependencies, credentials, error handling, observability, and recovery as production design concerns rather than afterthoughts. Use the subtopics—Validating Untrusted Input, Avoiding Hard-Coded Secrets, Safe Error Messages and Logging—as a checklist: predict what the example will do, then verify it in a project configured for the target platform.
content.why_it_matters: Professional applications need repeatable tests, clear APIs, dependable dependencies, security checks, and observable failures. Apply this concept in small steps before integrating it into a larger project.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Treat external input, dependencies, credentials, error handling, observability, and recovery as production design concerns rather than afterthoughts.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with validating untrusted input. Then compare it with avoiding hard-coded secrets. Identify the input, state, dependency, or branch that determines the result. The snippet is a static reference for CodeLeaf and is not executed in the lesson page.

items.title: Validating Untrusted Input
items.text: Validating Untrusted Input defines a trust boundary. Validate untrusted input at the boundary, keep secrets server-side, check authorization where the protected operation occurs, and test both allowed and rejected cases.

items.title: Avoiding Hard-Coded Secrets
items.text: Avoiding Hard-Coded Secrets defines a trust boundary. Validate untrusted input at the boundary, keep secrets server-side, check authorization where the protected operation occurs, and test both allowed and rejected cases.

items.title: Safe Error Messages and Logging
items.text: Safe Error Messages and Logging helps make behavior observable and repeatable. Define the expected result, include a boundary or failure case, and preserve enough diagnostic information to locate the cause without leaking sensitive data.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in the project that declares the necessary JVM, coroutine, networking, database, or serialization dependencies. Never commit real secrets.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the documented starting values, rerun the smallest test, and compare the result with the expected output. If behavior differs, check the compiler/plugin/runtime versions and the active target before changing more than one thing.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: Secure Kotlin Programming removes the need to test boundary conditions or verify the chosen runtime/library version.

content_blocks.title: Troubleshooting and reset
content_blocks.text: If the example fails, first confirm which runtime/project type the snippet requires. Read the first useful compiler or runtime message, check imports and declared dependencies, reduce the example to a minimal case, and rerun. For target-specific code, use the target toolchain rather than assuming a console or browser runner can execute it.

items.title: Explain
items.text: Describe the main rule of secure kotlin programming in your own words.

items.title: Apply
items.text: Change one input or condition and predict the result before running it.

items.title: Verify
items.text: Check one edge case and the official reference for the selected Kotlin/runtime version.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small variation that demonstrates secure kotlin programming. Write down your predicted result first, run it in the correct local project, then explain one boundary case involving validating untrusted input.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain secure kotlin programming without copying the lesson wording.
Demonstrate the concept with a small code/configuration change and state the expected result.
Test one boundary case or explain a relevant platform/version limitation.
hints: Begin with the first syllabus subtopic: Validating Untrusted Input. What input or state does it act on?
Change only one value, branch, declaration, or dependency at a time. Predict what should happen before running the code.
Compare your observed result with the expected output and the official reference; verify that you are using the required project type and dependency set.
